item.title: Lazy gas, hot gas, and a thousand robots
item.abstract: Amazon Robotics operates over a million robots across more than 300 warehouses worldwide. Inside a single warehouse, thousands of robots share the floor, moving inventory for order fulfillment and stock replenishment. Finding efficient, collision-free robot paths to their destinations is therefore essential for smooth operations. Let us formulate the underlying multiagent pathfinding (MAPF) problem a bit more precisely. Consider a typical warehouse layout as a W x H rectangular grid. At each time step, a robot can make one of five choices: move north, east, west, or south, or wait. These choices must be coordinated to avoid collisions. Over a planning horizon of T time steps, finding optimal robot paths involves approximately n = 5WHT binary decision variables, giving 2n possible combinations before accounting for feasibility constraints. Finding optimal paths that minimize the total move cost or arrival time without collisions is NP hard in general and can become computationally intractable even for moderate numbers of robots. In a paper we presented at this year’s International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), we show that physics offers a way around this intractability: plan trajectories as if the robots were particles of gas. Modeling the robots as a cold, lazy gas, whose particles spend only the minimum effort to reach their destinations, yields optimal, minimum-energy paths. This is equivalent to treating trajectory planning as an optimal-transport problem. It yields optimal paths, but computing them may take too long for real-time deployment. Modeling the fleet as a hot gas, whose particles jitter randomly along the way, yields trajectories that are computationally faster but potentially suboptimal. As the temperature drops to zero, however, the jittery hot-gas paths settle onto the lazy-gas ones. Our approach uses a Schrödinger bridge — a hot-gas model — to efficiently approximate the solution to an optimal-transport problem — the cold-gas model. Optimal transport To develop the formal connection, let us travel back to 1781 in France to meet Gaspard Monge, the father of differential geometry. Monge was looking for the most efficient way to transport excavated dirt to military fortifications. His studies gave rise to the optimal-transport problem, which asks how to transport resources from a set of sources to a set of destinations while minimizing cost, such as distance traveled or work done. Monge’s sources were the locations containing dirt. His formulation required all mass at each source location to be transported to one destination, producing a deterministic transport map. Although intuitive, Monge’s original formulation is a difficult nonlinear optimization problem with a potential combinatorial explosion in discrete settings. Finding an optimal map is therefore technically challenging and, in some settings, impossible. Roughly 150 years later, Soviet mathematician Leonid Kantorovich relaxed this restriction by allowing mass from one source to be split among multiple destinations. His key insight was that this relaxation converts a difficult optimization over transport maps into a linear program, a class of problems for which highly efficient computer algorithms were subsequently developed. Kantorovich received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for his contributions to the theory of optimum allocation of resources. Optimal transport connects two mass distributions, also known as marginals, through minimum-cost transport plans. This two-marginal formulation represents only the initial and final configurations and the cost of transporting between them, not the intermediate paths or collisions along those paths. Formulating MAPF as optimal transport therefore requires a multistage approach, because robots generally cannot move from their starting locations to their destinations in a single time step; their locations must also be represented at every intermediate time. We develop this connection in detail in our paper, using multimarginal optimal transport (MMOT), which extends optimal transport to a sequence of marginals. In other words, the additional marginals represent robot locations at intermediate times in MAPF, allowing motion to be modeled across both space and time. In the case of anonymous MAPF problems, where any robot can go to any destination, a key result we prove in the paper is the following: The MMOT formulation solves the combinatorial anonymous MAPF problem to optimality with a runtime of O(n1.68) seconds in practice and with a theoretical upper bound of roughly O(n3). Formally speaking, we achieve this by carefully preserving the total unimodularity of the underlying constraint matrices. We next provide a brief explanation of total unimodularity (TU). Consider the decision variables in a transport plan as a vector or a point in a high-dimensional space, with each coordinate specifying how much mass is transported from one grid cell to another in a single time step. The set of all feasible plans forms a geometric object called a polyhedron. Total unimodularity guarantees that every corner of this polyhedron has integer coordinates. Since a linear objective attains its optimum at a corner of the corresponding feasible polyhedron, a linear program (LP) provides optimal and integer solutions in polynomial time. Without total unimodularity, a linear program may return a fractional solution; for example, it may send half of a robot along one route and half along another. Going back to the scale of Amazon warehouses, a square 150 × 150 grid with 1,125 robots has 3.4 million decision variables over a planning horizon of T = 30. Our TU-preserving MMOT provides optimal robot trajectories from their starting locations to their destinations in 478 seconds. By contrast, the non-TU, NP-hard formulation often fails to find even a single feasible solution in 12 hours. Finding an optimal solution in 478 seconds, however, might still be impractical. A natural question is whether we can improve the solver’s runtime by accepting a slightly suboptimal solution. It is not generally clear how to formulate such a tradeoff in clean technical terms, which leads to our next contribution. Gases hot and cold The path to answering this question begins, unexpectedly, not with robots or linear programs but with Erwin Schrödinger and a cloud of hot gas in 1931 Germany. Schrödinger asked, Given the observed distributions of gas particles at two different times, what was the most likely evolution between them? The emphasis here is on most likely: hot gas particles diffuse randomly, through Brownian motion, rather than following deterministic paths. This “hot gas” characterization contrasts with classical optimal transport, which can be modeled as “lazy gas” diffusion, in which particles expend only the minimum work needed to reach their destinations. It turns out that the temperature of the gas provides the technical lever needed to traverse the spectrum from lazy gas (optimal but potentially longer runtimes) to hot gas (computationally faster but suboptimal trajectories). To relate Schrödinger's gases back to MAPF, we devised a probabilistic Schrödinger bridge between the initial and final robot configurations. Instead of selecting a deterministic set of paths, the bridge casts robot transport as a shadow, i.e., the most likely way for the robot mass to flow from one state to another. In our paper, we show that this is equivalent to an entropic relaxation of the MMOT problem. The amount of entropy added is analogous to the gas temperature and controls how much randomness is added to the robot trajectories. This allows us to extend a very fast method called Sinkhorn iterations to solve for the shadow. Because the shadows are probabilistic, they divide each robot’s mass across possible destinations in space and time. Since individual robots can’t split apart, we can’t execute this plan directly.

item.title: OpenAI and Cisco Releases Shirudo: An Open-Source Linux Runtime Allowing Agents to Defend Systems Without Downtime
item.abstract: OpenAI and Cisco have released Shirudo , an open-source Linux runtime for defending live systems. Shirudo is an eBPF runtime that lets AI agents write temporary “shields” against known exploits. Shields block the vulnerable behavior while legitimate requests keep flowing. Teams get time to test and ship the real patch. The engineering came from Isovalent at Cisco , the team behind Cilium and Tetragon. Patching takes time. OpenAI team notes that testing and deploying a fix can take days or weeks. Blocking a whole Linux operation is risky, because exploits and normal requests often share it. Shirudo targets that patch window. Shirudo uses eBPF, which runs small verified programs at hooks inside the Linux kernel. The name is Japanese for “shield.” Isovalent calls it a rewrite of Tetragon , its 2022 eBPF security platform. The design splits work across 2 roles: A shield can do 3 things. It can block the code path a bug needs, replace vulnerable code, or add detection visibility. The docs call these packages upatches : small BPF C programs shipped as signed artifacts. There is deliberately no policy DSL. The Linux Plumbers talk by Daniel Borkmann and John Fastabend says agents work better with code directly. Isovalent describes 4 stages, with Codex as the control plane: Operators approve shields before enforcement. Teams can also observe a shield’s impact before it blocks anything. The kernel checks each loader’s signature against a .bpf keyring. The eBPF verifier then checks program safety. A TPM 2.0 records every load and unload, and signs attestation evidence. The test bundle uses an ML-DSA-87 signing key, a post-quantum algorithm. Registry traffic uses TLS 1.3 with hybrid post-quantum key exchange. Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) is a heap corruption bug in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. It scores 9.2 on CVSS 4.0. It affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI. Calif.io found it on October 24 using Codex. Oracle shipped a fix on November 17. Codex generated a guard on java.util.Base64$Decoder.decode0 . It was attached to a running Elasticsearch 9.5.5 node. The exploit input was rejected and the service stayed up. That is the only disclosed test. No false-positive rate or overhead figure was published. Source note: OpenAI frames shields as eBPF. The Isovalent post says this specific shield was Java bytecode. The Java agent docs call such upatches an in-application mitigation, not a kernel boundary. Those docs also describe startup-time loading only, while the demo attached at runtime. Requirements are strict. Per the system requirements page : There is no fallback for older kernels. Developers can try the VM quickstart or the Isovalent lab . Check out the OpenAI announcement , Isovalent technical post , GitHub repo and docs . You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . item.title: Even the best AI agents struggle with everyday life
item.abstract: AI companies have spent the last couple of months marketing personal AI agents as tools to take over the digital drudgery of human existence — and millions have been sold on the vision, handing over their shopping schedules, travel plans, and everyday responsibilities to AI assistants. But new research suggests that even the most advanced AI models struggle to reliably and safely navigate the messy details of people’s lives. According to ShellBench, a new benchmark for everyday agent work, even the most advanced models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta failed more than a third of the time. Across all models tested, 15.7% of attempts failed at least one safety requirement, often leading to unintended consequences. ShellBench was developed in collaboration with researchers at The OpenClaw Foundation, Parsewave, Hugging Face, Red Hat, and UC Berkeley, drawing on more than 10 million anonymized, real-world AI agent interactions to see how agents perform on the everyday work people actually delegate to them. The research comes as personal AI assistants are finding new popularity among developers, with Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic all fighting for a piece of the market with Muse, Dots , and Claude Duet , respectively. In October, Meta said more than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada had set up its personal AI agent, Muse, within six weeks of launch, with about a quarter using it daily. That number is expected to grow as Meta implants Muse directly into Instagram DMs . Despite growing popularity among consumers, we still have little evidence about how reliable AI personal assistant products actually are. ShellBench suggests that the unreliable nature of most everyday data sources still causes problems for many state-of-the-art systems. A successful agent should be able to navigate messy personal workspaces containing emails, calendar entries, spreadsheets, receipts, chat logs, outdated information, and phishing attempts, and figure out which information is relevant, what is private, and how to deliver the requested outcome without creating new problems. It seems many of today’s AI agents are still not up to the task. Not only did even the highest-performing agents frequently fail to meet the requirements of a task, but they also lacked consistency. When researchers ran each task three times under identical conditions, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, the highest-scoring model, nailed all three attempts less than half the time. For autonomous assistants that are meant to run in the background without supervision, it’s a problem if users need to run an agent multiple times to get a result they trust. Additionally, about 10% of otherwise correct attempts failed at least one safety criterion. Across the models and harnesses tested, agents failed to, for example, adequately account for a child’s school pickup 79.5% of the time. When handling laptop custody records, agents failed a requirement to identify and withhold a sensitive bank upload token in 18.6% of attempts. In another task, agents recommended duplicate or incorrect invoice payments 40.3% of the time. The findings highlight a major issue for users adopting consumer personal AI assistants, namely that there’s always a risk that an agent can create more headaches in the course of trying to fulfill an otherwise ordinary request. While AI benchmarks have largely focused on coding, professional work, or testing on specific tasks, ShellBench is attempting to evaluate how models perform on multi-step personal tasks within different agent harnesses — the software that controls how a model accesses information, uses tools, and takes actions. While the researchers found model choice had a greater overall impact on performance than harness choice, among the more capable models, AI agent performance became more dependent on the harness. For example, OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra outperformed Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 when operating within the Pi harness, but it performed worse when both models were tested within Claude Code. Meta’s Muse Wonder Full scored 56% in Pi, but only 38.1% in Claude Code. Meta’s Muse Wonder 1.0, meanwhile, averaged a success rate of 39.7% across the five harnesses tested. Notably, while the researchers tested models from Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic, they didn’t evaluate them within the native harnesses of Muse, Dots, or Claude Duet, so the results may not be representative of the experience millions of consumers are having with the product today. TechCrunch has reached out to Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, and the researchers in the study.

item.title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
item.abstract: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system. “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said . Made for defenders, but attackers like it too Cairn is an open source AI problem-solving engine whose first validated domain is autonomous penetration testing. Users give it a task or goal and, optionally, hints for achieving it. A server maintains a shared graph containing facts and hints. A dispatcher reads the graph, schedules tasks, manages containers, and writes the protocol. The dispatcher can then assign each project to a dedicated worker container, each of which runs multiple agents concurrently. Cairn is model-agnostic and can be used on worker back ends, including Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Researchers from security firm Palo Alto Networks have also observed Cairn being used with GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and DeepSeek V4 Pro. Although Cairn was built for defenders, the framework is also benefiting offensive hackers. https://x2robot.com/docs/quantax1pro/v1/model-development/wallx-api/api-usage-instruction 過去幾年，整個具身行業一直在預訓練中苦苦找尋自己的大模型時刻，想要實現真正意義上的通用智慧。 如今，終於有頭部玩家憑底層技術和硬核的真機驗證，率先打破行業困局。 具身通用智慧，真的從技術共識走向現實了。 行業苦等多年的預訓練通用智慧，終於有了答案 通用智慧 放到今天，其實算不上一個很新的詞。 很多友友聽到它的第一反應估計是：這Astra那Fable的，各家大模型不早就把通用智慧卷翻天了嗎！！！ 確實啊，過去幾年大模型的狂飆，已經為整個AI行業驗證了一條極具確定性的技術路線—— 隨著 預訓練 資料和算力規模不斷擴大，模型能夠從海量經驗中學習通用規律，並獲得跨任務解決問題的能力。 按理說，順著這條被驗證過的路，具身智慧通往通用智慧的程序也該勢如破竹。 但現實，卻遠比想像中骨感，也更一言難盡。。。 大家應該都有一個共識，理想中的通用機器人，應該像人類一樣，能在各種陌生環境中靈活完成任務。 為了實現這種真正意義上的通用， 這幾年整個具身行業也都堅信「預訓練」是唯一的出路。 也正因如此，過去幾年從機器人基礎模型到VLA，預訓練逐漸成為具身領域最重要的技術方向之一。 但尷尬的是，行業對預訓練的信心越來越足，機器人自己的「通用智慧時刻」卻遲遲沒有到來。 其核心的問題，便在於模型所展示出的 泛化能力 上。 就拿經典之經典的Google DeepMind的RT系列模型來說吧—— 早期的RT-1，在熟悉任務上的成功率已經高達92%，可一旦進入陌生環境，成功率便驟降至20%。 即便後來升級到RT-2，引入更強大的視覺語言模型，面對陌生環境的成功率也只有49%。 模型越來越強，學到的知識越來越多，但面對陌生場景、指令和任務，機器人依然很難靈活應對： △Google DeepMind 說到底，過去幾年，整個具身行業對通用智慧始終處於一種 「既想要又得不到」 的尷尬狀態。 而就在整個行業苦苦求索之際，自變數團隊如今把這條路跑通了，併為行業給出了肯定答案： 預訓練，真的可以誕生通用智慧。 從WALL-OSS-0.5開始，自變數就在死磕通用這條路線，只不過如今真的把這件事做成了。 WALL-OSS-1.0通過視覺、語言與動作聯合預訓練，以及更大規模的資料學習—— 讓機器人不用任務微調，僅憑預訓練習得的能力，就能在陌生環境和全新任務上直接上手幹活。 具身行業苦苦追尋的預訓練通用智慧，如今終於從技術信念走向了真機驗證，所以，這到底是咋做到的啊？ 從預訓練到Scaling、Agent，機器人通用能力如何持續進化 動作前置參與預訓練，讓理解與行動共同進化 要弄明白WALL-OSS-1.0在通用智慧上的突破關鍵，還得先解開一個困擾具身行業多年的問題： 為啥大語言模型可以通過預訓練學會舉一反三，機器人卻常常換個任務就犯難呢？ 其實問題之一，就藏在過去許多VLA模型的 「訓練方式」 裡。 傳統VLA訓練，往往先讓模型學會識別物體、理解指令，再加入動作資料，教機器人如何動手操作。 聽著沒毛病，但問題其實就出在這兒，因為 等機器人真正開始學動手時，理解世界的方式早已基本定型了。 這就意味著模型雖看得懂任務，但未必能靈活操作，換個陌生環境或指令就可能宕機，又得重新微調： △AI生成 自變數機器人團隊，顯然更早意識到了這個問題，並且這次從訓練方式上動起了腦筋—— 既然模型的世界觀和手上的幹活本事老是碰壁有資訊差，那還等啥後期微調打補丁啊。。。 不如讓動作經驗從一開始就加入預訓練，和視覺、語言一起進爐修煉，共同塑造模型理解世界的底層能力！！ 具體來說，WALL-OSS-1.0採用了兩階段訓練法： 第一階段，讓視覺、語言和動作資料共同參與預訓練，讓機器人從一開始就把看懂世界和動手操作聯絡起來。 第二階段，再引入專門負責精細控制的動作專家，讓機器人動起手來更準、更高效。 這種先學理解、再練精細操作的分工，也正好也破解了小機器人幹活兒時「看得懂，卻幹不好」的老難題。 △AI生成 此外，為了讓動作真正融入預訓練，自變數還升級了X-Tokenizer，把複雜的動作軌跡壓縮成模型能理解的編碼。 這樣一來，機器人動作也能像文字一樣 Token化 ，和視覺、語言資料一起參與預訓練～ item.title: Meet Facebook’s Your Algorithm: How Meta Turns Plain-Language Preferences Into Ranking
item.abstract: Meta has published an engineering deep dive on Facebook Your Algorithm . Your Algorithm lets people tell Facebook, in plain language, what they want in Feed and Reels. Meta announced the feature on October 13, 2026. The new post shows how large language models (LLMs) sit inside a production recommender. For developers, it is a rare look at explicit preferences wired into an implicit-signal ranking stack. Your Algorithm is an AI-powered preference page for Facebook Feed and Reels. It has 3 parts, per Meta’s engineering post . A one-sentence “Lately Summary” describes recent viewing. An “Interested In” list is prefilled from past activity. A “Not Interested In” list holds exclusions. Users can type interests, move them between lists, or delete them. Access is through the three-dot menu on posts, according to Meta’s newsroom . Meta’s framing is simple. Implicit engagement signals scale well but adapt slowly and miss nuance. Explicit, stated preferences close that gap. Meta splits the preference lifecycle into 4 components: Validated interests are enriched with an embedding and search keywords. They are saved to a shared store that both Feed and Reels read. A separate component runs integrity and safety checks. Each interest drives 4 retrieval sources. 2 match content directly: search and clusters of closely related topics. 2 extend reach: the content graph and item-to-item similarity. A relevance check compares the interest’s meaning with each candidate. Passing candidates get a late-stage ranking promotion. A reranking control layer then stops flooding: Meta calls this layered filtering at every stage. Ranking uses embedding comparison to remove close matches. Demotion rules push down near matches. A fine-tuned LLM reranker then reviews the final list. Quality requests, such as less AI-generated or sexually suggestive content, take a different path. They map to dedicated demotion signals, not topic matching. Requests naming a creator filter that creator directly. On the client, cache invalidation removes queued items that match a new exclusion before display. The reranker is trained to return only the items to remove. Meta says this small fine-tuned model beat a general-purpose model judging each item. It was faster and more reliable. Outputting a short removal list is cheaper than scoring every candidate. Speed comes from a “supplementary tail load.” Adding an interest fires an extra fetch outside the normal cycle. Meta gives no latency figure for it. Source conflict: YouTube’s Help Center says 1 custom feed at a time. TechCrunch reports multiple feeds rolling out from October 2026. item.title: Three LLM inflection points in twelve months
item.abstract: I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I’d currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as “cheap Fable”). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they’ll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here’s Gemini 4 Neon’s attempt at “Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data”, for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don’t know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 “This game isn’t fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.” And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I’d used that appeared to understand fun. I’ve since worked on several little game projects where prompts like “Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful” produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I’ve been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they’d been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. I’m still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I’m getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I’ve been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 —plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 — all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements. If this does represent an inflection point, the key feature seems to be that if you can imagine and then clearly describe a piece of software, Fable can build it . That’s a wild thing to say, but it matches my experience over the past few weeks. Software development has transformed beyond recognition in the last year. I don’t think I’ll ever go back to typing most of my code by hand. This is Three LLM inflection points in twelve months by Simon Willison, posted on 24th November 2026 . item.title: How to Run Inkling 2 Mini Locally on an RTX 3090 Using Unsloth Studio
item.abstract: How to Run Inkling 2 Mini Locally on an RTX 3090 Using Unsloth Studio American open-source AI is making a comeback, and this powerful local LLM is proving that fast inference, AI coding agents, and impressive results don't require expensive APIs. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 24, 2026 in Language Models We finally have a serious American competitor to Qwen3.8-27B, one of the best AI models you can run locally. Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Mini , a powerful open-weight model that matches Qwen3.8-27B on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and even outperforms it on several coding, agentic, and tool-use benchmarks. What makes this release particularly exciting is its efficiency. Inkling 2 Mini has 26 billion parameters, but its Mixture-of-Experts architecture and innovative looping mechanism allow it to deliver impressive results without requiring expensive enterprise hardware. It is also designed for fast inference, with additional speed improvements possible through speculative decoding. The best part is that you can run a 4-bit quantized version on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 with 24GB of VRAM. This makes it an interesting option for developers and vibecoders who want a capable local model without depending on paid APIs. In this tutorial, we will run Inkling 2 Mini on an RTX 3090 using Unsloth Studio and put it through a few practical tests. We will generate a financial dashboard, build a playable 2D endless-runner game, and connect the model to the Pi coding agent to see how well it handles real coding tasks. 1. Install Unsloth Studio First, we need to install Unsloth Studio. It provides a simple web interface for downloading, running, and testing AI models locally without dealing with complicated setups. You don't necessarily need an expensive GPU for this. You can use a smaller GPU or even your system RAM, depending on the quantized version of the model you choose. However, for this tutorial, I am using an NVIDIA RTX 3090 with 24GB of VRAM. To get started, open your terminal and run the following command: curl -fsSL https://unsloth.ai/install.sh | sh The installer will automatically detect your system and install the required components. During installation, you might be asked whether you want to start Unsloth Studio immediately. For now, select n , as we need to configure a few things first. Start Unsloth Studio now? [Y/n] n Next, restart your terminal shell so that the newly installed commands are available. exec bash Now, let's configure where our downloaded models and cache files will be stored. AI models can take up quite a lot of space, so it is better to keep everything in one location. For this tutorial, we will store them in a folder inside our home directory. export HF_HOME="$HOME/models/huggingface" export HUGGINGFACE_HUB_CACHE="$HF_HOME/hub" export XDG_CACHE_HOME="$HOME/.cache" You can change these paths depending on where you have free storage. Just make sure you have enough space for the model you plan to download. Finally, start Unsloth Studio using the following command: unsloth studio -H 127.0.0.1 -p 8080 This will start the server on port 8080. On the first launch, you may be asked to create a password to access the interface. Once the server is running, open your browser and visit: http://localhost:8080 You should now see the Unsloth Studio interface, where you can download models, chat with them, and adjust different settings. That's it. We have successfully installed Unsloth Studio. Next, we will download and load Inkling 2 Mini using a 4-bit quantized version that can fit on our RTX 3090. 2. Load and Test Inkling 2 Mini Once Unsloth Studio is running, open the web interface and log in using the password you created earlier. You will see a simple interface where you can chat with models, enable tools, and adjust different settings. To get started, click on the model selection menu and search for Inkling 2 Mini . Select the model, and Unsloth Studio will automatically download and load it for you. For this tutorial, we are using unsloth/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF with the UD-Q4_K_XL quantization, which works well with our RTX 3090. The download might take a few minutes, depending on your internet connection. Once it's done, the model will be loaded automatically, and you can start chatting with it right away. For our first test, we enabled web search and asked the model whether we should buy NVIDIA stock. The model searched the web, gathered information from different sources, and gave us a detailed answer pretty quickly. It was interesting to see a local model handle a research-heavy question so well. We were also getting around 52 tokens per second on average , which is quite impressive for a model running on a single RTX 3090. Next, we wanted to try something more interesting. We asked the model to build an oil market dashboard that tracks different oil prices and indices. For this test, we disabled the tools because we wanted the model to generate the website directly without relying on Python or other tools. The result was surprisingly good. It created a clean dashboard with different oil price indicators, charts, and other useful information. What impressed me most was that the dashboard looked and behaved like a live market dashboard. It simulated price movements and updated the numbers even though the actual markets were closed. Of course, these were simulated values rather than real-time market data, but the overall design and functionality were really good. 3. Connect Inkling 2 Mini to the Pi Coding Agent Now that we have tested the model in Unsloth Studio, let's take things a little further and use it with a coding agent. For this, we will use Pi, a lightweight terminal-based coding assistant that can help us build applications, write code, and work on projects directly from the terminal. First, install Pi using the following command: curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh Once the installation is complete, restart your terminal shell: exec bash -l Next, go back to Unsloth Studio and open the API settings. You will find the connection details and API key needed to connect your local model to Pi. Unsloth also provides a command that makes this process quite simple. Copy the command from your setup and run it in the terminal. For Linux, it should look something like this: export UNSLOTH_STUDIO_URL="http://0.0.0.0:8080" unsloth start pi --api-key YOUR_API_KEY --model unsloth/Inkling-2-Mini-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL Make sure to replace YOUR_API_KEY with your own API key. If Unsloth Studio is running on another machine, use that machine's accessible server address instead. That's it. We can now use Inkling 2 Mini directly from our terminal through the Pi coding agent. To see how well it performs, I decided to give it a more challenging task. I asked it to build a 2D endless-runner game inspired by Subway Surfers, with animations, obstacles, collectible coins, and other visual effects. Here is the prompt I used: Create a fully playable, visually stunning 2D Subway Surfers-style endless runner game using HTML5 Canvas, CSS, and JavaScript, featuring three-lane movement, jumping, sliding, trains, obstacles, collectible coins, power-ups, smooth character animations, parallax scrolling city backgrounds, colorful cartoon graphics, particle explosions, glowing effects, motion blur, speed trails, dynamic lighting, screen shake, realistic shadows, sound effects, background music, increasing difficulty, collision detection, score tracking, responsive keyboard and mobile swipe controls, animated menus, pause and restart functionality, and polished arcade-style gameplay optimized for 60 FPS, using original characters and assets. The model started generating the code, and within a few minutes, we had a playable game that we could open directly in our browser. The result was actually pretty impressive. Compared to the basic 2D game we created earlier, this version looked much better.

item.title: [AINews] Jensen Is Back! and OpenAI Shows Its Pretraining Curve, joined by Microsoft
item.abstract: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation , and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4 , their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back . Eleven days after announcing his resignation , Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting ). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control. As Matt Levine points out , with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record. In Perplexity and Intelligence , Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their internal held-out coding dataset … which has notable caveats ): Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly . Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70. This is all in context of pacing the frontier . Pachocki proposes that labs agree on a first limit to development and spell out what would let them cross it, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitoring. Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman gave the first win by cosigning and joining in, running MAI-2 Base on OpenAI’s evaluation set and reporting 0.819. We’d need at least a couple more top labs to join this effort for it to gather steam as a real self-regulatory limit, most notably of course, Anthropic. Sponsored by Backblaze B2 If your data is growing faster than planned, you need storage that grows with your business, feeds flash and GPUs with terabit-scale throughput, and doesn’t charge egress. Backblaze B2 has delivered capacity tier storage for twenty years, manages more than six exabytes, and is trusted by leading neoclouds, labs, and gen AI companies. Growth shouldn’t be something you sweat. We’ve got room for whatever you’re building. OpenAI Publishes Its Pretraining Perplexity History and Proposes Shared Development Limits The disclosure : Jakub Pachocki's essay "Perplexity and Intelligence" publishes five years of OpenAI base-model log-perplexity on a fixed held-out dataset. It argues for industry-wide limits based on perplexity and other measurements, with further progress gated on milestones in understanding and monitoring AI behavior, such as a successor to chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors ( essay thread ). Policy framing : Sam Altman quoted the proposal for a first common limit with concrete exit criteria ( quote ). He tied it to the standards commitments in the White House Accords ( accords ). Endorsements : Greg Brockman highlighted the warning that alignment progress is unlikely to keep pace with pretraining acceleration ( gdb ). Mark Chen called the numbers formerly "sensitive IP" and asked other labs to disclose their key metrics ( markchen90 ). Claimed findings : Losses below 0.8 coincided with emergent capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics ( excerpt ). Thresholds and timing : OpenAI expects further "transformative capabilities" in the ~0.68–0.7 window and describes a steep acceleration in 2026 ( summary ). Internal model : An unreleased internal model already sits below GPT-6.2 Astra. Pachocki says pretraining could see an "avalanche" like the recent one in math as soon as 2027 ( scaling01 ). Community extrapolations (unofficial) : Dan Hendrycks infers ~3–5×/yr compute-efficiency gains since GPT-4, possibly 100×+ this year ( hendrycks ). One fit, using the internal model at 0.732 against 0.761 for the released model, reaches 0.70 between January and March 2027 ( fits ). Microsoft joins : With OpenAI's permission, Microsoft AI reported MAI-2 Base at 0.819 on OpenAI's eval set. It shares OpenAI's tokenizer and lands in GPT-5.6 Sol base-model territory. Mustafa Suleyman suggested bits-per-byte for future cross-lab comparisons ( mustafasuleyman ). Open-model mapping : Elie Bakouch used MAI as a bridge to place open models on OpenAI's curve ( plot ). He labels the further chaining through Inkling bpb a "very weak approximation" ( details ). Lucas Beyer's caveat : Inkling's held-out codebase may be largely agent-generated, which would make bridge-based placements look too optimistic ( giffmana ). Methodological critiques : Critics raised several confounds: Tokenizer bias : Common limits could favor OpenAI over Anthropic because of tokenizer differences ( davidmanheim ). Post-training compute : Post-training likely accounts for more than 75% of FLOPs, so pretraining perplexity may be the wrong pacing metric ( stochasticchasm ). Synthetic data : Part of the steep curve may come from a growing share of model-generated pretraining data ( Azaliamirh ). Missing context : Without model sizes or compute figures, it is hard to separate scaling from algorithmic progress ( Grad62304977 ). OpenAI's response : Staff say the eval is fixed over time and excludes model-generated code ( johnohallman ). Will Depue added that it is "held out, frozen, tokenizer agnostic" ( willdepue ). Pressure on other labs : Several researchers asked OpenAI to release the held-out set ( oneill_c ; DimitrisPapail ). Anthropic's redactions : Anthropic redacted pretraining metrics from its METR report ( eliebakouch ), prompting calls to publish them ( _NathanCalvin ). Third-party verification : METR offered to verify pause or compute-allocation claims under its standard terms ( ChrisPainterYup ). Frontier Model and Product Launches: Gemini 4 Neon, GPT-6.2 Sol, Claude Ship Gemini 4 Neon : Google positions Neon between Carbon (hardest long-horizon work) and Hydrogen (fast execution), aimed at complex coding and enterprise workflows ( Google ). Leaderboard results : Neon claims several top spots: LiveBench 2.0 : #1 at 87.4, versus 84.9 for both Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra, at roughly a quarter of Fable's cost per task ( LiveBench ). AI Chess Leaderboard : #1 at 1924 Elo ( chess ). Arena text : Google holds the top three, with Carbon at 1527, Argon at 1520 and Neon at 1513 ( Arena ). Adoption signals : OpenRouter spend on Google models exceeded OpenAI's for the first time since June ( OpenRouter ). Perplexity traffic : Neon is compounding +10.6%/day in Ask and +15%/day in Computer. Aravind Srinivas says this is organic switching from Opus 5.5 and Sol 6.2, not default routing ( growth ; clarification ). Access rules : Gemini subscriptions work only through the Antigravity binary. T3 Code is allowed because it wraps Antigravity; shims such as Pi are not ( theo ; Google confirmation ). Quota changes : Antigravity quotas were reset. Pro users get Carbon, and Hydrogen opens to all users ( _mohansolo ). Workspace : Neon is rolling out to Workspace customers in the Gemini app ( OfficialLoganK ). Hydrogen pricing : Hydrogen costs $1.50 per million input tokens. It scores 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, against 50 for Argon, and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 ( dl_weekly ). API features : New file slicing lets agents upload once and pay only for the pages, cells or clips Gemini inspects ( googledevs ). Function results can now return documents, audio and video natively ( _philschmid ).

item.abstract: 螞蟻OceanBase釋出湖庫一體AI資料平臺OceanLake，核心引擎向全球開源 量子位的朋友們 2026-11-24 11:30:46 來源： 量子位 中國AI資料平臺加速崛起 11月24日，螞蟻OceanBase AI資料大會在北京召開。OceanBase CEO楊冰在會上表示，當模型越來越先進，Agent基建越來越成熟，挑戰終將回歸資料。面向這一變化，AI時代的資料基礎設施應堅持“湖庫一體、多模融合、Agent友好、開源開放”四大原則。圍繞這一方向，OceanBase正式釋出AI戰略產品——湖庫一體AI資料平臺OceanLake，並宣佈向全球開源其核心引擎AI資料庫，邀請開發者和產業夥伴共同建設面向AI的資料基礎設施。 楊冰認為，當前企業的智慧化轉型遠不及預期。其一，模型能力的商品化已經完成，能力迅速提升、成本持續下降，模型本身不再是瓶頸；其二，“低枝果實”已被摘完，公共資料的價值挖掘殆盡；其三，新的業務飛輪尚未形成，業務與資料的相互促進和協同進化尚未實現。 他進一步把企業資料生產力釋放的困境概括為“三座冰山”：第一座在私有資料與公有資料之間——沒有私有資料的價值挖掘，就沒有生產力的真正釋放；第二座在多模態資料與結構化資料之間——多模態資料將帶來更多的價值增量；第三座在亂資料與有序資料之間——整理亂資料是釋放資料生產力的必要條件。 在楊冰看來，AI時代的資料基礎設施應堅持四大原則：一是“湖庫一體”，統一儲存全量業務資料，還要支援離線、線上一體化計算；二是“多模融合”，能基於業務語義，對多模態資料進行統一治理，通過混合搜尋成為可計算、可利用的資產；三是“Agent 友好”，具備效果觀測與評測、長期與共享記憶、許可權治理等能力，支撐Agent的規模化執行和自我進化；四是“開源開放”，支援開放計算和多模型呼叫，適配多種基礎設施和異構晶片混合部署，以應對複雜的計算環境和快速變化的技術需求。 基於這一判斷，OceanBase在會上正式釋出面向AI時代的戰略產品——湖庫一體AI資料平臺OceanLake。OceanLake採用湖庫一體架構，融合資料庫的即時事務處理、資料倉儲的分析計算與資料湖的開放儲存能力，統一管理結構化、半結構化和非結構化等多模態資料。企業可以在同一開放平臺上開發和治理資料，開展離線批次加工，並將加工成果直接用於線上分析、檢索和Agent應用，實現離線上一體。 OceanLake AI資料平臺將多模態資料與企業的業務定義關聯起來，用真實業務資料和知識開發、評測Agent，為生產任務提供即時業務上下文，支撐Agent從開發驗證走向規模化應用，回應多模態資料為AI所用、AI理解業務、Agent可靠服務、全員便捷用數四類問題。 目前，OceanLake的能力已在多個產業場景落地，覆蓋多模態資料處理、Agent應用和資料智慧等環節：為螞蟻靈波、靈心巧手等打通多模態資料處理與模型訓練鏈路；支撐螞蟻靈光超過3000萬個“閃應用”執行，並將螞蟻阿福的模型評測環境準備時間從天級縮短至分鐘級；幫助平安壽險用AI“讀懂”保險，實現員工輕鬆“對話經營資料”，將典型取數交付時間從2—5天縮短至約15分鐘，並支援廈門航空通過 DataPilot讓財務資料“開口說話”，實現“經營問數決策”。 同時，OceanBase AI資料庫也正式開源，這是一款面向Agent場景的湖庫一體資料庫，開源專案代號為OceanSeek。OceanBase AI資料庫採用湖庫一體架構，將資料庫的即時讀寫和分析能力與資料湖的開放儲存相結合，支援多模態資料管理、混合檢索和資料沙箱，幫助企業高效開發、評測和執行Agent。至此，OceanBase 已形成完整的開源體系——從2021年開源核心資料庫能力，到2025年釋出並開源 seekdb，為本地開發和端側AI應用提供輕量、可嵌入的資料庫。此次開源的OceanSeek則進一步拓展到企業級AI應用與Agent場景。OceanBase堅持開源，持續邀請全球開發者與從業者共同建設，持續降低產業使用門檻。 在技術趨勢上，楊冰認為，當AI進入生產級，資料庫的核心能力將變得更加重要和進一步被進化，16年根自研是OceanBase在AI時代的最大底氣，從資料庫到AI資料平臺，資料庫的核心能力正在被賦予新的內涵：一致性，從分散式一致性走向多模態資料一致性；可靠性，從核心業務系統可靠性走向 AI 生產業務可靠性；擴展性，從一個庫承載海量資料，走向海量小庫縮容至零；即時性，從即時 HTAP 走向即時 Agent 決策。 楊冰表示，技術在變，需求在變，真正不變的只有對高品質確定性環境的追求。他說，去年我們提出做資料庫是個良心活，從那時起的十多個月，AI浪潮把大量資料難題衝到面前，對OceanBase而言這並不陌生——16年前，我們相信做好資料就是做好了移動支付；5年前，我們相信做好資料就是做好了核心系統現代化；現在，我們相信做好資料就是做好了人工智慧。“從AI資料庫到AI資料平臺，是這場技術長征的第一步，未來我們將永遠保持專注，做好資料這件事。” item.title: Responding to objections to recursive self-improvement
item.abstract: Okay, so I recently released this essay and this video about recursive self-improvement and why I expect superintelligence by 2030. A wild claim, and understandably, lots of people had objections. Many of them are actually quite interesting and compelling, and I want to go through them here. And by the way, I’m joined by Max Farrens , who is my General Manager, and we ended up discussing all of these ideas as we were writing them down. And in fact, we paired in a lot of the writing. I think a good place to start is with a comment on the Substack version of the post that comes from a user named Jim, who writes as The 1690 Project. “Dwarkesh, do you have a real job where you use this stuff” (meaning AI) “in and day out? I am guessing you do not, because I do, and this is not what I am seeing at all.” What do you think? Those are two different questions. Do I use these things day in, day out? Yes. Do I have a real job? Debatable. Don’t answer that. Funny that the guy’s like bragging about having a real job. He’s like, he’s like a gotcha on me. Like, I’ve been one of the main people who for the last year and a half has been arguing that the basic learning capabilities that these models lack do in fact impair their productivity. I think people who a naive understanding of what it means to automate a job just look at a system like GPT-6 and say, oh, why can’t we have AGI? It can automate all the white-collar work. I think this is totally wrong. The point I’m making in this essay is that are currently worse than humans at almost everything, right? IT is 1% of the economy, well-scoped coding tasks is a small fraction of IT. In some things, AIs are in fact getting to human level or beyond human level, where we have lots of verifiable proxies. And I would argue that just like math, AI research has a lot of verifiable proxies. And so the consequences of narrow progress in AI research or towards AIs that can do AI research leads to general improvements in AI capabilities. So if you look at a system like GPT-3 and you compare it to GPT-6, GPT-6 is also narrow intelligence, right? It can solve Millennium Prize problems, but it can’t be my video editor. So it can do basically everything way better than GPT-3. What I am imagining is that disproportionate progress in ML research, or AIs that are good at doing ML research, will compress as much progress as we had between GPT-3 and GPT-6 into a single year. And so the end result is within a year of having a system like GPT-7 or GPT-8 or whatever it ends up being, we end up with systems that are more generally capable in the way that humans are generally capable, and are on track to then rapidly become better than humans at everything. So Cindy Wu writes on X , “Dwarkesh conveniently sweeps under the rug that climbing a metric involves defining it. Supposing you define it in a way that avoids Goodharting, reward hacking, etc., you need data and environments which do the lifting on defining good metrics. This is most of the game of making AGI, converting fuzzy concepts to formalized objects you can climb without gaming, which requires costly fixes later. He elides the hard problem by saying AI will just automate data.” I think there’s two parts to Cindy’s objection here. One is: can we find metrics which capture general AI progress? Are we aware of such metrics? And two, will we be able to generate the data that makes AIs good at getting better at those metrics? A big part of my essay was dedicated to articulating what those verifiable proxies for general AI progress are, right? So in pre-training, the loss on a held-out corpus is not only a proxy for pre-training progress, it is the basis of pre-training progress, and that is extremely verifiable. And there’s a lot of other proxies you can come up with that are just general intelligence capabilities that are kind of agnostic for any given paradigm. For example, how fast do you master a video game you’ve never seen before? This is one of the key ways that humans are different from current AIs, that humans master new video games really rapidly. How fast can an AI that has only seen a data corpus up to 1700 figure out general relativity? How many open math problems can it solve, right? So there’s a lot of paradigm-agnostic, hard metrics of progress we can come up with. The second argument here is learning algorithms. The application of learning algorithms is very general. The transformer was invented to beat the existing state of the art in translation, but because that architecture, or the implications of the architecture, were general, it also was really good at predicting the next token in WikiText. It’s also really good at generating images and so on. And similarly with reasoning models. Initially they were invented and they were debugged to, like, solve high school math problems and simple coding problems, and now they’re applicable and useful across lots of different domains. And so the breakthroughs that are made in AI end up being measurable on lots of different metrics. And the reason they’re measurable across lots of different metrics is because AI, or intelligence, is general, and because of that, its general improvements show up and make contact with reality in lots of different ways. So you started out by saying that there were two subpoints you wanted to address. The first is around verifiable proxies, and I think I understand that your answer is something of the sort of: it is not just that there are verifiable proxies that we can hill-climb, they are, like, the things themselves that we can work on. And so AI research makes itself particularly amenable to hill climbing. The second is around how we actually get the data to do that sort of work, and that is the part I don’t think I understand. So I’d be curious what your thoughts are. Yeah. So it is true that data is a big part of AI progress. The question is, what is the nature of those data improvements? And it seems to be the case, based on external evidence, that the nature of those improvements are the things that ML researchers who are not experts in any domain other than ML research are able to do. So when you look at how do pre-training data improvements happen, I actually did some research on this. We ended up spending probably on the order of, like, tens to maybe $100,000 of GPUs on this. Hopefully it was worth it just so I can say this one comment, which is, we did this study about, if you look at data corpuses from... Well, this is Jerry Han, by the way, who’s a student at Princeton. And we did the study: if you look at data corpuses from 2019 up till 2026, and then you look at architectures from 2019 till 2026, which explains why we’ve gotten better at pre-training? And we found that actually data explains more of the progress than the architectures. But what we found is that if you look at how that data has gotten better, so that people have released public datasets of pre-training over time, the main improvements are just better methods for filtering data and better methods for coming up with synthetic data. And this is just work that ML researchers are doing on their computers, who are not experts in Shakespeare or quantum mechanics or whatever is in the pre-training corpus. They’re just doing empirical science about, hey, if I filter the data this way instead of that way, will my end model be better at solving math problems? If I make synthetic data this way instead of that way, will my end model be good at doing law or whatever? And so this is just, like, bread-and-butter ML research work. To jump in, just: you mean as opposed to having to hire a bunch of experts in law and then a bunch of experts in banking and a bunch of experts in... to generate a bunch of, like, very sort of specific examples, it is more that these ML researchers, who themselves may know nothing about these domains, can do it alone. Exactly. Now there is a question about: can you automate those ML researchers?

item.title: Data Modeling Best Practices for an Agentic CDP, Part 1: The Data Foundation
item.abstract: A customer saved a jacket to their wishlist on your site 9 days ago. This morning its price dropped 30%. Should you let them know? That depends on your goal. If you want first-time buyers to come back for a second purchase, the alert could help. If you're growing lifetime value and this customer usually pays full price, the discount may cost more than it earns. Whatever the goal, an agent needs six answers about this one person before it makes the call (Figure 1). Figure 1. The goal frames one price-drop decision, and the decision needs answers from six kinds of data. If you're getting customer data ready for an Agentic CDP, start here. At Databricks, we work with many brands on this, and the data model is usually the hardest part. This post is for the data architect who designs the stack that marketers, and now agents, build on. This is Part 1 of a two-part series. Part 1: the modeling steps, from raw data to omnichannel activation. Part 2: mapping B2C and B2B datasets, attributes and use cases onto the model. An Agentic CDP needs everything a traditional CDP needs: the right sources, clean data, one identity per customer and golden profiles marketers trust. If you've built a CDP before, that work carries over. If you haven't, it's the place to start. What changes is who does the work and how fast the data has to be right. Agents take on more of the work, such as matching records and drafting audiences, while people choose the sources, review the matches and approve what goes out. And because an agent decides for one person in seconds, a gap in the data turns into a bad decision just as fast. What it means for your data model A segment, refreshed on a schedule A decision for one person, on demand Each attribute resolves to one trustworthy value per person Owned, explainable and reversible An identity graph you can audit, with a persistent ID Deep history plus what's happening now Batch and event data keyed to the same ID Rules people set and agents check before each action Consent, suppression and business definitions stored as data Teams and agents adjust daily from measured results Engagement and outcomes land back in the lakehouse, with holdouts Databricks built CustomerLake around the same idea. Data teams can define trusted datasets and models once through Databricks and Unity Catalog. Marketers can then use purpose-built interfaces to ask questions, build segments, and activate audiences faster without working around IT or exporting data into unmanaged tools. Here's the flow we recommend. It's a medallion architecture with one important rule: identity resolution runs after silver, and the canonical ID it creates becomes the join key for gold. You build the layers with Spark Declarative Pipelines , keep them on schedule with Lakeflow Jobs and govern every layer in Unity Catalog . Figure 2. One governed path from raw data to connected channels, keyed by one canonical ID. Brands have asked for years why they can't own their identity graph and run deterministic matching on their own data. The usual answer was upkeep: the rules, reruns and reviews take people and time. With identity resolution running next to the data, owning the graph becomes practical, and in our experience it's the most important table you'll build. Figure 3. Four source records resolve to one person. The id_graph keeps the rule and confidence behind each link. Run deterministic rules first (exact email, exact phone, a partner ID that maps to your customer ID), then score the gaps with probabilistic matching. Then cluster the matches and mint, or keep, a persistent ID. You can build this with SQL rules plus an open-source matcher such as Splink or Zingg. Or use CustomerLake: Profile Agents handle the heavy lifting of matching and golden-record survivorship. The approach is called Agentic Identity Resolution, which combines deterministic, probabilistic, and LLM-based matching to connect fragmented records. Manual data steward overrides allow teams to apply human judgment where needed. Figure 4. Use attribute columns directly; aggregate or filter behavior tables first. Keep the full consent history (one row per person, channel, purpose, source and time) and the suppressions, such as unsubscribes and bounces, in silver. Derive the 1:1 consent table from them, so audiences and agents check one place before they send. Flag each gold table so campaign builders know how fresh it is: Updated incrementally as events arrive, one row per event with a timestamp Web and app events, cart, transactions In-session decisions, filters and triggers Build event tables as streaming tables in Spark Declarative Pipelines and record the flag as a Unity Catalog tag . Streaming tables can update on a schedule or continuously; for triggers like a cart reminder, run their pipelines in continuous mode, which "keeps tables fresh as new data arrives." Behavior that arrives only on a schedule, such as nightly store sales, stays Batch until you stream it. If the events carry the canonical ID, adding triggers later shouldn't need a remodel. Two more habits help: compute time windows against a declared as-of date, so a rerun gives the same answer, and keep one governed copy, giving each activation tool only the tables it needs. With the model in place, you define an audience or a decision once, on governed gold tables, and send it to the channels your customers use. Figure 5. Decide once on governed data, activate across channels, and land responses back as data. CustomerLake enables direct syncing of audiences and signals to martech, adtech and CX channels directly with native Reverse ETL connectors, without custom pipelines or additional activation layers. If you can say yes to most of these, your foundation is ready for agents: The foundation is in place. In Part 2, we put it to work: We'll come back to the jacket use case in the beginning, and show which datasets answer each of the six questions. 1. What is the best data model for an Agentic CDP? A medallion architecture where identity resolution runs after silver and its canonical ID becomes the join key for gold. The gold layer has three kinds of tables: a customer table with every activation identifier, 1:1 attribute tables for model scores, consent and derived attributes, and 1:many behavior tables, such as orders and events, at event grain. 2. Where should identity resolution run in a CDP data pipeline? Identity resolution should run in one place, after data is cleaned in silver and before the gold layer is built. Running it on normalized emails, phones and addresses gives more accurate matches. It should rerun as new records arrive and publish a persistent canonical_id plus an auditable identity graph that records the rule and confidence behind each link. 3. Why should brands own their identity graph? An owned identity graph is explainable, auditable and reversible, and agents need that to make decisions for one person safely. Brands can run deterministic rules first, score the gaps with probabilistic matching, and record merges and splits so downstream systems can follow. With identity resolution running next to the data, keeping the graph up to date is now practical. 4. What is the difference between attribute tables and behavior tables in a CDP? Attribute tables have one row per customer, holding values like propensity scores, consent status or lifecycle stage. Behavior tables have many rows per customer, one per event with a timestamp, such as orders, web visits or service cases. Marketers use attribute columns directly and aggregate behavior tables into new attributes, such as "orders in the last 30 days." 5. How do you prepare a CDP data model for real-time, trigger-based campaigns? Flag each gold table as batch or event, and build event tables as streaming tables keyed to the canonical ID. For triggers like cart recovery, run those pipelines in continuous mode.

item.title: Introducing preemptible compute: the same compute, half the price
item.abstract: Try now → Preemptible compute is now generally available on Together GPU Clusters, on Kubernetes and Slurm clusters in all regions. Preemptible nodes give teams a lower-cost way to run interruption-tolerant work — short experiments, inference bursts, batch jobs — on the same GPU infrastructure they already use, billed sub-hourly at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate. You can add preemptible capacity to a new or existing cluster starting today. How preemptible compute works Preemptible compute adds a second compute type to Together GPU Clusters. Standard nodes are fulfilled synchronously and are never preempted. Preemptible nodes use the same NVIDIA accelerated compute, draw from un-used capacity, and can be reclaimed when that capacity is needed elsewhere. Preemptible nodes are billed at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate. The rate remains fixed rather than moving with a spot market. When a node is reclaimed, the cluster follows a five-minute drain (maximum 5 minutes) sequence: T+0 — the node is cordoned, a TogetherPreemptionNotified Kubernetes event fires, and your pods receive SIGTERM. T+0 to T+5:00 — your workload has up to five minutes ( terminationGracePeriodSeconds ) to checkpoint and exit. T+5:00 — the node is removed. The cluster retains its preemptible target after the node is removed and automatically refills toward that target as capacity becomes available. You do not need to request replacement capacity. Billing is sub-hourly, with usage metered every one to two minutes. A node that runs for 12 minutes is billed for approximately 12 minutes. Preemptible nodes are not a separate cluster type. They join your existing cluster, labeled together.ai/compute-class=preemptible , so interruptible workers run on discounted capacity while coordinators, login pods, and serving replicas stay on standard nodes. Where preemptible compute fits The five-minute reclamation sequence makes recovery behavior the deciding factor. Work that can resume, retry, or requeue can use preemptible capacity while critical components should remain on standard nodes. Short experiments. Ablations, config sweeps, quick fine-tunes, evals, distillation, and batch inference are good candidates when the work can resume from a checkpoint or retry after a worker disappears. Frameworks such as Ray Train and PyTorch Lightning resume from the latest checkpoint without intervention. As a reference point, a full weight model checkpoint for GLM5.3 Flash, 321B parameter model is roughly 3.5TB which would take between 22s to 4mins to write to a parallel filesystem even at degraded performance. Leaving headroom inside the five-minute drain window. Temporary bursts. When batch or internal inference demand spikes, add cheaper preemptible nodes to absorb the burst and non-critical workloads instead of holding standard capacity sized for your peak or risking burst standard compute availability. Interrupted requests requeue; user-facing replicas remain on standard nodes. The common thread: work that is chunked, checkpointed, or retryable. Multi-day runs without checkpointing and strict-SLO serving with no fallback are not a fit. Together has a strong culture dogfooding , several internal research, dev/test and non-critical production workloads at Together are based on our preemptible compute based GPU clusters enabling us to leverage our spare capacity across product teams. Before you enable it Treat preemptible nodes as ephemeral. There is no minimum node lifetime, so checkpoint frequently and plan for capacity to disappear at any time. Keep critical components on standard nodes. Coordinators, login pods, and user-facing replicas belong to guaranteed capacity — use the compute-class label to enforce it. Use the drain window. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to as much as 300 seconds, checkpoint when the pod receives SIGTERM, and exit before the node is removed. A cluster can run entirely on preemptible nodes. Keep at least one standard node if you need your shared storage reachable at all times. Nodes can't be converted between compute types in place. How to use it After the workload is prepared for preemption, setup has two parts: set the preemptible target and schedule eligible work onto the labeled nodes. You can set the target when creating a cluster or on a cluster that is already running, using the Together Cloud console, CLI, or API. The API reports both the requested target, desired_preemptible_gpus , and the capacity currently live, allocated_preemptible_gpus . Because preemptible nodes draw from unused capacity, allocated capacity can remain below the desired target when capacity is tight. On a new cluster Choose your standard node count, then add a preemptible target on top. tg beta clusters create \ --name my-cluster --region us-central-2 --gpu-type RTX_6000_PCI \ --cluster-type KUBERNETES --num-gpus 8 --billing-type ON_DEMAND \ --num-preemptible-gpus 8 \ --project-id <proj_id> On an existing cluster Scale up the preemptible target when you need additional worker capacity, then lower it when the work is complete. The cluster remains running throughout. tg beta clusters update <cluster-id> --num-preemptible-gpus 16 Fig: Adding/Deleting Preemptible nodes to an existing cluster Fig: Preemptible nodes follow the “gpu-preemptible-xxx” naming convention Scheduling work on preemptible nodes Target preemptible nodes explicitly: nodeSelector: together.ai/compute-class: preemptible Preemption notices are delivered as SIGTERM to the pod, as Kubernetes events ( reason=TogetherPreemptionNotified ), in the console's Event Timeline, and via the Together API's node_lifecycle_events — handling patterns are covered in the docs . Preemptible compute is generally available on Kubernetes and Slurm clusters. → Create a cluster → Read the docs

item.title: Active intrusion campaign against Check Point security management servers
item.abstract:
GreyNoise tracks threat activity using our Global Observation Grid (GOG), a sensor network designed to attract adversarial scanning and exploitation attempts on our managed infrastructure. One might think of these sensors as conventional “honeypots,” but that doesn’t quite capture the variety, versatility, and scale at which we deploy and manage the complex fabric of the GOG. Unsolicited activity against our sensors is sketchy if not outright nefarious, and our approach allows us to capture end-to-end intrusions and analyze a broad swath of attacker infrastructure, tools, and tactics in near realtime, without waiting for lengthy incident response investigations. We fuse data from our sensor network with additional novel sources and methods to develop a comprehensive picture of adversaries. ‍ Campaign Summary GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally. We are tracking this set of threat activity as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13) which represents adversary infrastructure, tools and post-exploitation action against the 22 victims. The campaign targeting does not appear to be focused on any specific geography or industry sector. The impacted orgs include victims with assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia, and the United States. The victim orgs sit in sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. We do not attribute GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group at this time. We do not currently have enough information to make assessments relating to the motivation of the actor or alignment to a nation-of-origin. The actor used 99 IP addresses, much of which were disposable network infrastructure to conduct scanning, exploitation, and control of its victims, including the use of a compromised server acting as an “operational relay box” (ORB) or more simply, a “hop,” for interacting with downstream victim assets. The actor used this relay box / hop to save command results and data stolen from 24 distinct Check Point Security Management Servers. The actor used Nmap , Chisel , Impacket , Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. The threat actor used or attempted to exploit multiple CVEs, including, but not limited to: CVE-2026-61500 (Rejetto HFS), CVE-2025-5777 (Citrix NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2026-41089 (Windows NetLogon), CVE-2026-16232 (Check Point SmartConsole auth bypass to Run Script), and CVE-2026-98432 (Linux IPv4 UAF). Though we observed hands-on-keyboard activity, we believe that like most modern attacks, the actor used LLMs and agentic systems to perform vulnerability scanning, exploitation, tool development, and automated interaction with compromised assets. Our visibility into this attack activity stopped around November 2nd, 2026, but given the actor’s persistent access to victim Check Point devices, we expect that this intrusion campaign is ongoing. We are working with international government partners and CERTs to share relevant intelligence and notify the victims. ‍ Observed Attacker Activities We witnessed the GT13 actor use 99 IP addresses, all of which were either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices, including activity over 1400+ network sessions, 800+ command line artifacts, and 1200+ files downloaded, uploaded, or created. We cannot cite all of the details here, but we can highlight observed GT13 adversary activities to illustrate their tradecraft and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). ‍ HFS Scanning and Exploitation The GT13 threat actor used an automated scanning and exploitation pipeline to compromise an HFS server using CVE-2026-61500 . 2026-10-02 13:17:45 UTC - The actor scanned and began exploitation against the HFS server. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returns a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm, and thus recover an HFS session-cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allows the attacker to login as admin without a password. Example POST to loginSrp1 and response Decoded hfs_http blob from 200 OK response showing the sid that is harvested ‍ 2026-10-02 13:19:37 UTC - Minutes later, we observed admin requests with forged session cookies, leading us to believe this exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The actor now had control of the server. Example HTTP POST request with forged cookie ‍ Note that this forged cookie contains “allow_session_ip_change:true” which does exactly what it sounds like, letting the forged cookie work from any IP address. This is perfect for an adversary behind a VPN or operating from multiple exits. 2026-10-05 12:21:30 UTC - A few days later, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. On October 8th, we observed the actor’s automation check in to the compromised server using HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Then there was a lull in activity until October 19th. ‍ Establishing the Operational Relay Box / Hop 2026-10-19 14:53:48 UTC - We don’t know why (possibly a problem with the multi-agent architecture), but the actor did not use the SSH access right away. Instead, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. At this point, we can see that the actor intended to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations. Example of HFS command, which was preserved on the compromised server. ‍ Example decoded base64 blob demonstrating that the actor was intending to download an apparent “ZULT” Linux implant to the compromised machine. The malware download failed, and the adversary attempted to troubleshoot the download by checking running processes, invoking curl to access the resource, and viewing the network configuration. Example of the actor following up, attempting to check on their implant They couldn't figure out why their implant did not download, and the actor returned the next day with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay. 2026-10-20 07:22:08 UTC - The actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_<redacted>.py) which set up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, after which the actor began to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point Security Management Server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets. The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel , and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy. ‍ Intrusion Operations and Exfiltration Once the actor had the compromised server set up as a relay, they began to use it to manage their interactions with their previously compromised victim Check Point devices. There’s a lot of commingled victimology here, so we’ll refer to two sets of victims.
